title: Frontend tests with Vitest
intro: Frontend tests give you confidence that your React application behaves correctly from a user's point of view. In this lesson, you'll learn how Vitest and React Testing Library fit into a Vite + React + TypeScript project and how to test forms, asynchronous UI, and user interactions.
body:
## Why frontend tests matter

A frontend can compile successfully and still be broken for users. A button may not trigger the expected action, a form may accept invalid data, or a loading state may never disappear after an API request.

Frontend tests give you a fast way to verify that important user-facing behaviour keeps working as the application changes.

For a Vite + React + TypeScript application, a common combination is **Vitest** for running tests and **React Testing Library** for rendering components and interacting with them. Vitest is designed to work well with Vite's configuration and module system. You can find its documentation at [vitest.dev](https://vitest.dev/).

The important idea is that these tools have different responsibilities:

- **Vitest** runs the tests and provides assertions, mocks, test lifecycle hooks, and watch mode.
- **React Testing Library** renders React components and provides queries for finding elements.
- **user-event** provides realistic interactions such as clicking, typing, and selecting.

## Start with behaviour, not implementation

React Testing Library follows an important philosophy: test your application the way a user experiences it.

Instead of asking whether a component has a particular internal state, ask whether the user can see the expected result.

For example, imagine a login form. A useful test says:

> When the user submits an empty form, an error message appears.

A less useful test might inspect an internal React state variable and verify that it changed from `false` to `true`.

The first test is connected to real behaviour. You can completely rewrite the component internally and the test can remain valid as long as the user experience stays the same.

This is one reason React Testing Library encourages queries based on the accessibility tree and visible content.

## Finding elements like a user would

Prefer queries that describe how a user or assistive technology would find an element.

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "Which query should I use?", "caption": "Prefer the queries at the start: they find elements the way users and assistive technology do.", "steps": [{"label": "getByRole", "sub": "button, heading, textbox …"}, {"label": "getByLabelText", "sub": "form fields"}, {"label": "getByText", "sub": "visible content"}, {"label": "getByTestId", "sub": "last resort"}]}
~~~

For example, a labelled input can be found by its label:

~~~tsx
<label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" />
~~~

A test can then use a label-based query rather than depending on an implementation-specific CSS class.

Buttons and other interactive elements can often be found by their role and accessible name:

~~~ts
screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' });
~~~

Other useful queries include:

- `getByRole` for buttons, headings, links, inputs, lists, and other semantic elements
- `getByLabelText` for form controls associated with a label
- `getByText` when visible text is the important part of the behaviour
- `findBy...` queries when an element is expected to appear asynchronously

Avoid using `data-testid` as your first choice. A test ID is not inherently bad, but it is usually less meaningful than a role, label, or visible piece of text.

For example, this is preferable:

~~~ts
screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create task' });
~~~

rather than:

~~~ts
screen.getByTestId('create-task-button');
~~~

Use test IDs when there is no good user-facing or accessible way to identify an element.

## Setting up Vitest

A Vite project can use Vitest with a configuration that integrates with the existing Vite setup. A typical configuration might look like this:

~~~ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vitest/config';
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  test: {
    environment: 'jsdom',
    globals: true,
  },
});
~~~

The `jsdom` environment provides a browser-like DOM so that React components can be rendered during tests.

Your package scripts might include:

~~~json
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "vitest",
    "test:run": "vitest run"
  }
}
~~~

Running `npm test` starts Vitest in watch mode. Running `npm run test:run` executes the tests once, which is useful in CI.

## Testing a form

Forms are especially valuable to test because they combine user input, validation, and state changes.

Suppose a component contains a task title input and a submit button. A useful test can:

1. Find the input by its label.
2. Type a task title.
3. Click the submit button.
4. Check that the new task appears.

With React Testing Library and user-event, the test can resemble a real interaction:

~~~ts
const user = userEvent.setup();

await user.type(screen.getByLabelText('Task title'), 'Prepare report');
await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add task' }));

expect(screen.getByText('Prepare report')).toBeInTheDocument();
~~~

`user-event` is useful because it models interactions more realistically than manually changing DOM properties. Typing into an input is not just one assignment to `.value`; real browser interaction can involve several events.

For validation, test what the user sees. If an empty title should produce an error, verify that the error message appears and that the task was not added.

## Testing asynchronous UI

Modern applications frequently fetch data after rendering. The test should wait for the UI to reach the expected state instead of relying on arbitrary delays.

~~~compare
{"left": {"title": "Asserting too early", "lang": "ts", "code": "render(<Tasks />);\nexpect(screen.getByText('Buy milk'))\n  .toBeInTheDocument(); // ✕ still loading", "note": "The data has not arrived yet."}, "right": {"title": "Wait for it", "lang": "ts", "code": "render(<Tasks />);\nexpect(await screen.findByText('Buy milk'))\n  .toBeInTheDocument();", "note": "findBy… retries until the element appears or times out."}}
~~~

For example, imagine a component that initially displays `Loading...` and later displays a list of tasks.

A synchronous query such as `getByText` is appropriate when the element should already exist. For asynchronous content, use a `findBy` query:

~~~ts
expect(screen.getByText('Loading...')).toBeInTheDocument();

const task = await screen.findByText('Prepare report');
expect(task).toBeInTheDocument();
~~~

`findBy` queries wait for the element to appear and reject if it never does within the configured timeout.

For a component that calls an API, you can mock `fetch` directly for a small focused test. For larger applications with many API interactions, **Mock Service Worker (MSW)** can intercept network requests and return realistic responses without changing the component's production code. The important principle is to test the UI resulting from the request rather than testing the mock itself.

## Test loading and error states too

A successful request is only one possible outcome.

A useful component test often covers at least three states:

- loading: the user sees a loading indicator
- success: the returned data appears
- failure: the user sees a useful error message

For example, if a task list displays `Loading tasks...` while waiting for a response, your test can verify that state first and then wait for the loaded task.

Similarly, simulate a failed request and verify that the application gives the user a meaningful message instead of silently doing nothing.

These tests are especially valuable because asynchronous UI bugs can otherwise be difficult to reproduce manually.

## Keep component tests focused

A component test should normally verify one meaningful piece of behaviour rather than every implementation detail.

Imagine a task filter component. You do not need separate tests for every internal state variable. Instead, test scenarios such as:

- all tasks are visible initially
- searching for `report` only shows matching tasks
- selecting `done` only shows completed tasks
- selecting `open` only shows incomplete tasks
- a filter with no matches shows an appropriate empty state

These tests communicate the component's contract very clearly.

They also make refactoring easier. You can change `useState` to another implementation, split the component into smaller components, or change CSS classes without rewriting the tests if the user-visible behaviour remains the same.

## Snapshot tests

Vitest also supports snapshot testing. A snapshot records a representation of rendered output and compares future test runs against it.

Snapshots can be useful for stable output where seeing a broad structural change is genuinely valuable. However, they should be used sparingly.

A large snapshot can become difficult to review. Developers may update the snapshot automatically without noticing that an important UI change slipped through.

For most interactive components, explicit behavioural assertions are clearer:

~~~ts
expect(screen.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Tasks' })).toBeInTheDocument();
expect(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })).toBeEnabled();
~~~

These assertions tell you exactly what behaviour matters.

Use snapshots when they provide useful signal, not simply because they are convenient.

## Watch mode and CI

During development, watch mode is extremely useful. Vitest can rerun affected tests as you edit source files.

A typical workflow is:

~~~text
Change component
    ↓
Vitest detects the change
    ↓
Relevant tests run
    ↓
Fix the failure
    ↓
Continue developing
~~~

When your tests run in CI, you usually want a non-interactive command that finishes with a success or failure status.

For example:

~~~shell
npm run test:run
~~~

Your CI system can then fail the build if a test fails.

This creates an important feedback loop: local development catches problems quickly, while CI prevents broken code from being merged unnoticed.

## Common mistakes

### Testing implementation details

Avoid testing private state, internal helper functions, or exact component structure when the user does not care about them. Prefer observable behaviour.

### Using test IDs everywhere

`data-testid` can be useful, but if an element has a good accessible name, role, or visible text, use that instead.

### Waiting with arbitrary timeouts

Avoid tests such as `await new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 1000))`. They make tests slower and can still be flaky. Use asynchronous queries such as `findBy...` when waiting for UI changes.

### Only testing the happy path

A form that works with valid data but crashes on invalid input is still broken. Test validation, loading, empty, and error states where they matter.

### Making snapshots enormous

Large snapshots are difficult to understand and easy to update blindly. Prefer small, meaningful assertions about user-visible behaviour.

### Forgetting CI mode

Watch mode is excellent during development, but CI needs a command that runs once and exits. Keep a dedicated command such as `vitest run` for automated builds.

## What to remember

The goal of frontend testing is not to prove that every line of React code executed. The goal is to gain confidence that important user interactions continue to work.

Use Vitest as the test runner, React Testing Library to query the rendered UI, and user-event for realistic interactions. Prefer accessible queries and asynchronous waiting over implementation details and arbitrary delays.

When you write a test, imagine a real user performing the action. If your test describes what that user sees and does, you are usually testing at the right level.
takeaways: Vitest provides the test runner and development workflow for Vite-based projects.
React Testing Library encourages tests based on what users can see and interact with.
Prefer roles, labels, and visible text over test IDs and implementation details.
Use user-event for realistic interactions and findBy queries for asynchronous UI.
Keep snapshot tests small and purposeful, and run tests once in CI.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of Vitest in a Vite + React project?
options: To replace React components with HTML
To run and manage automated tests
To provide the application's REST API
quiz.explanation: Vitest is a test runner and testing framework that integrates particularly well with Vite-based projects.

quiz.question: Which query is generally the best choice for finding a Save button?
quiz.explanation: A role and accessible name closely represent how a user or assistive technology identifies the button.

quiz.question: When should you generally use a findBy query?
options: When the element is guaranteed to exist synchronously
When an element is expected to appear asynchronously
quiz.explanation: findBy queries wait for matching content to appear, making them useful for asynchronous UI such as fetched data.

quiz.question: Why should snapshot tests generally be used sparingly?
options: They cannot be executed by Vitest
They only work with backend applications
Large snapshots can be difficult to review and may hide meaningful changes
quiz.explanation: Snapshots can become large and noisy, making it easy to approve changes without noticing an important behavioural regression.

quiz.question: Which command is most appropriate for a non-interactive CI test run?
quiz.explanation: A command based on vitest run executes tests once and exits, making it suitable for CI.

exercise.title: Build a testable task filter
exercise.task:
Create a React task-filter component that is accessible and therefore easy to test. The application must contain a text input labelled "Search tasks", a select labelled "Status" with the options "all", "open", and "done", and a
    with aria-label="Tasks". Render only tasks matching both filters from a fixed list of exactly five tasks defined in the code. The list must contain at least two completed tasks and at least two task titles containing the word "report". Display a

    containing the number of matching tasks, such as "3 tasks" or "1 task"; when there are no matches, display exactly "No tasks match". The starter contains the fixed data and the basic application structure but does not implement the filtering or status correctly. Make the UI respond to typing in the search field and changing the status select.
exercise.hint: Compute a filtered array from the fixed tasks. Compare the lowercased, trimmed search text with each title, then apply the selected status: all accepts every task, open accepts tasks where done is false, and done accepts tasks where done is true. Render the filtered array instead of the original tasks array, and derive the status message from filteredTasks.length.

tests.name: It renders the accessible filter controls and all five tasks initially
It filters tasks by the Search tasks label
It filters completed tasks when Status is changed to done
It combines search and status filters
It shows the no-match state
